headline: Agent Fleets Need a Control Plane for security and governance, like Kubernetes
summary: Managing AI agents in production requires robust control and admission gates to prevent over-budget runs and silent performance degradation. This approach mirrors Kubernetes' success in container orchestration.
details: Managing AI agents in production can lead to unexpected costs and risks without proper oversight. One field test demonstrated how a control plane instantly halted an agent that exceeded its budget, proving its critical value.

The core idea draws from Kubernetes' success: defining a desired state as a contract and using admission gates to enforce it. This involves workload manifests for each agent, specifying owner, tools, model identity, budgets, and certification thresholds.

While the ecosystem is moving towards Kubernetes CRDs for agents (kagent, agent-sandbox), these solutions primarily offer placement and isolation. They don't fully address the operational question of an agent's permission to run or its ownership when issues arise.

The real challenge lies in preventing agents from silently drifting or regressing in performance without changing their manifest. A robust admission gate must monitor actual work and compare verdicts, not just changes to configuration.

Certification acts as a crucial security control, not merely a quality metric. By binding production admission to signed attestations of exact model identity, common attack vectors like model swapping or quiet regressions are blocked and auditable.

Effective governance requires speed; if saying 'no' takes too long, controls are bypassed. A system capable of inspecting and stopping agents in milliseconds, and scaffolding new fleets quickly, ensures compliance and prevents costly workarounds.

headline_marked: [[Meta's AIRA agent wins Kaggle gold]] in NVIDIA Nemotron Challenge, ranking 8th out of thousands
headline: Meta's AIRA agent wins Kaggle gold in NVIDIA Nemotron Challenge, ranking 8th out of thousands
summary: Meta's AI agent, AIRA, achieved a gold medal in a real Kaggle competition, demonstrating how dedicated training environments and strategic agent refinements can significantly boost AI performance.
details: Meta's AIRA AI agent has achieved a gold medal in a real Kaggle competition, the NVIDIA Nemotron Challenge, ranking 8th among thousands of teams. This success demonstrates the significant impact of dedicated training environments and iterative agent improvements.

The journey began with AIDE, an earlier agent, which achieved a 35.2% medal rate on the MLE-bench lite dataset. This benchmark, created by OpenAI, uses 75 real Kaggle problems to test an agent's ability to write code and submit solutions.

By simply moving AIDE into the newly developed AIRA-dojo training environment, without any changes to the agent itself, its performance jumped to 45.9% on the lite set. This 10.7 percentage point increase highlights the crucial role of a well-configured and optimized training infrastructure.

Further improvements involved refining the agent's "operators"—the core instruction sets for task execution like drafting, debugging, and improving solutions. This led to an improved 45.5% medal rate on the lite set using the DeepSeek-R1 backbone.

The team also experimented with search policies, testing Greedy, Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), and Evolutionary strategies. The combination of AIRA with a Greedy search policy on the o3 model achieved a new high of 47.7% on the lite dataset, proving that even complex search strategies benefit from well-designed operators.

In early 2026, AIRA2 was introduced, featuring a distributed architecture running on eight GPUs for parallel processing. It also expanded benchmarks to include MLE-bench-30 and AIRS-Bench, adopting Percentile Rank as a key metric to gauge performance against human leaderboards.

AIRA2, using the Gemini 3.0 Pro Preview model, achieved an average Percentile Rank of 71.8% on MLE-bench-30 within 24 hours, extending to 76.0% with 72 hours. An updated version with Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview further boosted this to 81.5% in 24 hours.

An ablation study revealed that the "Human-Competitive Evaluation" (HCE) system, which provides reliable feedback without revealing test solutions, was the most critical component. This underscores that effective feedback mechanisms are more impactful than simply increasing parallel processing power.

The culmination of these efforts is AIRA3, which secured a gold medal in the NVIDIA Nemotron Challenge on Kaggle in September 2026. This final system utilized an ensemble of GPT 5.5 and Claude 4.8 models to enhance the reasoning capabilities of NVIDIA's Nemotron 30B model.
